content:
Earlier this year, I replaced a petrol lawn mower with a robotic mower that can be controlled via iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the lawn boundary to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe this machine may be easier for many people to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 that I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each robot understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map out the lawn, with no need to bury boundary wires or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I feel it may be simpler for people who are not very familiar with computer technology.

To verify this claim, I asked my mother — who lives in another state — to install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She said everything worked fine. However, I'm not entirely sure whether she would have the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire boundary with her phone and mark out all the areas that need to be avoided.

The automatic mapping caused a small issue at my front yard. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when creating the initial map.

A peek through the mower's camera

The TerraMow's cameras also bring one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used the iPhone's screen mirroring function to keep this view open in a large window on my Mac. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting and can sometimes explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share quite a lot in common. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone division, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice variation on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, with no human intervention required. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is quite interesting for tidying up small patches the robot missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (the fun kind). I walk beside the mower holding the iPhone, move my thumb just slightly, and the robot follows my command.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder in operation.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow 'noisy', but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly — so quietly that you almost forget it's still running, even when it's mowing at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow comes with a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while the Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for daily mowing for several consecutive weeks, during which no human intervention was needed at all.

When adaptive mapping becomes too clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower keeps adjusting the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you cannot perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. A puddle formed somewhere in the yard, and TerraMow reasonably avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret the growth there as an object to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, that area continued to be skipped.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower over to cut the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once the area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along faint boundary lines might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. That method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids situations where the map 'changes its mind' about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac Conclusion

Having used both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying wires underground is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining additional hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, unclear property boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a patch of overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, a captivating real-time camera view, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I have used.

I do enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot frees up time for tending the garden, edging, and handling detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs excellently in this regard, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but do not want to bury wires underground, install an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard with their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, which is the price after applying a US$200 coupon on the website. The product is also available on TerraMow's official website.
